title: DGCA to Probe ATC System After Air India Flight's False Hijack Alert
excerpt: The pilot of Frankfurt-Delhi flight AI2030 denies sending the 7500 hijack code that forced a diversion to Jaipur, putting Mumbai ATC's new systems under investigation.
body:
• India's aviation regulator, the DGCA, will investigate the air traffic control system itself after Air India flight AI2030 was diverted to Jaipur on October 14 following a hijack alert that proved false.
  • The pilot-in-command has denied ever transmitting squawk code 7500, the transponder signal for unlawful interference, raising the possibility of a technical error in Mumbai ATC's new systems.
  • All 306 people on board — 293 passengers and 13 crew — were safe; the Boeing 787-9 was cleared after security checks and reached Delhi at about 3:10 p.m. the same day.
  • Travellers on the Frankfurt-Delhi route face no schedule change from the incident, but the probe's findings will matter for anyone flying through Mumbai-controlled airspace, where the alert originated.

India's Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) will examine the air traffic control system for a possible technical error after an Air India flight from Frankfurt to Delhi was diverted to Jaipur on Wednesday, October 14, over a hijack alert that turned out to be false. The investigation shifts the focus of the incident from the aircraft to the ground systems that ordered it down.

Flight AI2030, a Boeing 787-9 carrying 293 passengers and 13 crew, landed at Jaipur International Airport at about 9:35 a.m. and was moved to an isolation bay for security inspections, according to officials cited by The Hindu BusinessLine. Passengers were taken to the terminal, the aircraft was searched, and after clearance the flight departed Jaipur in the afternoon and landed in Delhi at about 3:10 p.m.

A Signal the Pilot Says He Never Sent

The diversion was triggered when Mumbai air traffic control received squawk code 7500, the internationally recognised transponder signal indicating hijacking or unlawful interference, while the aircraft was in the Mumbai Flight Information Region. What makes the incident unusual is the dispute over where that signal came from.

"The investigation shifts the focus of the incident from the aircraft to the ground systems that ordered it down."

According to Jagran, the pilot-in-command denied squawking the code at all, and told controllers when they made contact that there was no hijacking on board. Security protocol nevertheless required the diversion, and both sides have maintained their positions since. A separate source cited by BusinessLine likewise said the pilot did not activate the code and had informed Ahmedabad ATC, which sits under the Mumbai region, of that fact — while other security sources attributed the activation to a technical glitch.

Why the ATC System Is Now Under Probe

A senior official has said the DGCA will investigate the incident, and Jagran reported the regulator will specifically probe the new systems at Mumbai ATC for a possible technical error. That question matters beyond one flight. Mumbai's controllers handle traffic for Delhi and western India on routings that have grown longer because of geopolitical airspace restrictions, so a false alert generated or misread by ground systems would be a systemic concern, not a one-off.

Air India said the flight was diverted following a perceived security concern and that the relevant security agencies carried out the necessary checks and cleared the aircraft and crew. Passengers reboarded the same aircraft with the same crew for the onward journey to Delhi.

What Passengers Experienced

A passenger on board, Swasti Rao, a professor at OP Jindal University, told Hindustan Times, as reported by Jagran, that the pilot informed passengers ATC had directed the diversion to Jaipur without initially explaining why, and that the crew returned every ten minutes with updates. After landing, the pilot told passengers the alert had been a hoax.

What Happens Next

The DGCA investigation will need to reconcile the transponder and ATC records: whether code 7500 was transmitted by the aircraft, generated by a glitch, or misattributed by ground systems. Until the regulator reports, the incident stands as a case study in how aviation security protocol is designed to act first and ask questions later — a diversion, isolation-bay search and full passenger screening are mandatory responses to a 7500 signal, whatever its source.
